analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 9, Youngstown Sheepton Truth Company, Bellant, versus Stanley J. Bowers, Tax Commissioner of Ohio. We'll wait a moment. Mr. Dargis, you may proceed now. The court, please, Youngstown Sheepton Tube Company, versus Bowers, number 9, and Allied Stores of Ohio, Inc., versus Bowers, number 10, are appeals from the Supreme Court of Ohio. The Youngstown Sheepton Tube case involved the question of the Ohio State taxation of imported ores and storage merchandise held by a resident manufacturer. The Allied Stores case involves only the question of the Ohio State taxation of storage merchandise held by a resident retail merchant. Since the facts in the two cases differ somewhat, I will argue first the Youngstown case and then the Allied case. More specifically, the questions presented in the Youngstown case are, may an Ohio State statute constitutionally impose an ad valorem tax upon bulk iron ores which have been imported from foreign countries and which were stored in the same form as imported and not commingled with other property of the taxpayer? As to the second question of the taxation of storage merchandise, does an Ohio State statute,ено 195701.08 revised code of Ohio deny residents of the State an equal protection of the laws under the Constitution of the United States by imposing an ad valorem property tax upon residence storage merchandise held for storage only while at the same time accepting the storage merchandise of non-residents when similarly held for storage only? Those are the two questions, if the court plays in the Youngstown case. Mr. Thomas, you will tell us the particularity of facts before you get off the call? Yes, sir. I plan to do so. Maybe, sir, can I? The constitutional questions involved. First, Article I, Section 10, Clause 2, no state shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties that has been construed to include taxes on imports or exports except that which may be necessary, absolutely necessary, for executing its inspection laws. The second constitutional provision involved is Section 1 of the 14th Amendment. No state shall deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws. Basically, the laws of Ohio, and I'm referring specifically to 5709.01 Revised Code, lay a tax on personal property which is located in Ohio and used in business in that state. At this point, it might be well if I explain the provisions of old Section 5701.08 Revised Code, which are an issue in this case. That section was amended effective September 30, 1955, but we are concerned here with the statute as it read before that date. That section imposed a tax upon the storage of property, or upon property stored, with the proviso, but agricultural products and merchandise belonging to a non-resident, and held in a storage warehouse for storage only in this state, are not used in business. So the property of the non-resident was excluded by that provision, while the property of the resident was taxed by the general provision taxing property held for storage. The section, as I said, has since been amended, the distinction between resident and non-resident withdrawn by the general assembly, and a further limitation provided in that for property to qualify as being stored in Ohio and accepted from taxation, it must have been shipped from without the state, held for storage in the state, and destined for shipment outside. That issue is not in the case, but I wanted to point out the court statute has been amended. The history of this case is that the tax commissioner for the year 1954 assessed the imported iron ore and storage merchandise of the taxpayer. On appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals, the Ohio State Board of Tax Appeals, the imported iron ore was excluded from taxation, and the storage merchandise was taxed. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Ohio, both the imported iron ore and the storage merchandise was held taxable. At every stage in the proceedings, we raised the constitutional questions which we present to the court today. Now, the facts have been stipulated. The Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company imported ore from five foreign countries. Brazil, Cuba, Mexico, Liberia, and Canada. The ores from the first four, in other words, Brazil, Cuba, Mexico, and Liberia, were purchased for ultimate use in the appellant's open-hearth furnaces, while the Seine River Ore, or Canadian Ore, was purchased for use in the blast furnaces of the taxpayer. Yes, sir. Thirty-three, Justice Brennan. And printed in the brief as well at page three in part. In the movement of the ores from Brazil, Cuba, Mexico, and Liberia, the ores were transported by ocean vessel to either Baltimore or Philadelphia. They were unloaded at those ports and then transported by rail to Youngstown, Ohio, where they were stored in the storage yards of the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company. So far as the Seine River Ore, or Canadian Ore, was concerned, that ore was transported down the Great Lakes to Cleveland, Ohio, and then over the state of Ohio by rail to Youngstown, Ohio, and the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company. And as these ores were received in Youngstown, they were placed in piles. And as we received additional shipments of Brazilian ore, for example, and the same applies to all the ores, that particular type of ore, that identical ore, was placed upon the prior shipment. But there was no commingling of Brazilian with Liberian, Cuban, Canadian, or Mexican. In other words, the ore pile, at all times, contained only Brazilian ore. What was the purpose of keeping them in those different piles? Because of their characteristics, Mr. Chief Justice Warren. Because of their characteristics. Characteristics? Yes, sir. They weren't used for the same purpose? Normally not. Normally not. The characteristics of the ores that require them to be kept separately. They differ in their chemical composition. As I noted in my statement of facts, for example, the Seine River ore was used wholly in the blast furnaces, while the other four classes of ore were used in the open hearth. But for metallurgical reasons, the iron ores were kept separate in their several piles. From time to time, and as needed by the taxpayer, the ores in these five different piles were moved from the storage yard a substantial distance to the plant of the taxpayer, or the manufacturing facility, if you please, where they were either placed in what are known as the stock houses or stock bins that are pertinent to the blast furnaces and open hearth. But there are in the record maps showing the area over which these ores would travel from their storage yard to the stock bins or stock houses. May I ask you, sir, was that one day supply or more than one day supply that would be moved from the piles to these bins within the mill at one time? The stipulation shows that the storage piles represented a minimum of three months' supply, and that as needed, ores were moved to the stock bins and stock houses. The period of supply there would be relatively short, a matter of days at the outside. That is, you will see that in the stipulation, I believe. The piles, the piles would be the fungible goods for their respective piles. Yes, sir. In bulk. In bulk. And the piles, what would be the duration of this continuing pile? From the incoming shipments, is there any... There is nothing in the record on that point. As a matter of fact, you left now seven months... That's right. And all was added and kept a minimum of three months' supply in the pile. We'll recess now.
